1.label: Played a slow/passive move or wrong move-order that wastes a critical tempo, when concrete action was needed — most often in pawn/king endgames (let the opponent reach a key square or make a break first). Holds across BOTH bands: TOP = endgame tempo/move-order errors (a5 blocks own king, delayed f5 break, Kc2-before-bxa4); MIDDLE = 'purposeless king move', 'pure tempo loss', 'slow non-essential pawn move'. Tempo theme persists peak-to-middle (not peak-only), so not over-specialized.

6.label: A capture/trade that breaks a favorable tactical situation by relieving the tension — often a wrong-move-order capture (took before the intermediate check/zwischenzug) or trading off the attacker. Median boards are clearly tension/move-order driven; peak adds queen-trades that squander a winning attack.

3.label: Best move is a capture in ~100% of boards — a hanging enemy piece the player declined. At peak activation the captured piece is overwhelmingly the queen (94% of the high-activation cohort); across the full firing range it broadens to rook/knight, so 'often Queen' names the peak, 'hanging piece' the general case.

4.label: The played move is a check 100% of the time (20/20), but it's never the best move (best-is-check 0%) and usually loses material (hung-own 85%) — a check that achieves nothing and backfires.

5.label: Self-inflicted opening blunders where an aggressive premature piece sally hangs material (lost own material 100%, best move never wins/captures); top boards are blatant full-piece hangs—usually a knight thrown to g5/e5 or queen to h5 that's snapped off for free (Ng5→Qxg5, Qh5→Nxh5)—while median boards are subtler self-inflicted losses, dropping a pawn or walking into a fork/discovered attack rather than hanging an entire piece outright.

11.chip: Losing Rook/Queen Trade into Pawn Endgame
11.label: The piece captures/swaps off the last rook (72%) or queen (28%), liquidating a difficult-but-holdable rook or queen endgame into a lost king-and-pawn ending (best move was to keep pieces on); top boards are clean, decisive losing trades (avg ~270cp swing into K+P), while median boards degrade into milder/near-zero rook-placement and king-safety errors that aren't true liquidations.

9.chip: Missed Defensive Capture, Allowed Discovered Check
9.label: The recurring mistake is failing to capture an intruding enemy knight with the h-pawn (hxg6/hxg3) — the only saving move — which lets that knight grab the rook on h8/h1 while uncovering a queen check along the h5–e8 (or h4–e1) diagonal; the TOP boards are the near-identical Qh5+Ng6 discovered-check motif where hxg6 was forced, while the MEDIAN boards generalize to ignoring the single forcing defensive resource in more varied positions (hanging pieces, trapped pieces, positional collapses).

7.label: In won/winning endgames the player overlooks a free, undefended enemy piece (a rook in ~75% of cases) that the best move would simply capture, and instead plays an idle king/pawn push or meaningless check that throws away the win; the top boards are stark missed-free-captures with massive 900–1700cp+ swings (winning→drawn/lost), whereas the median boards are softer, more varied positional/technique slips (wrong recapture, failing to cut off the king with the rook, walking into a fork) that merely bleed an advantage rather than dropping a whole piece.

2.label: A loosening pawn push that weakens the player's own king cover. Pawn-move dominant at strong activations (24/25 top, 20/25 upper), broadening to rook/bishop moves only in the weak tail. Unlike a walk-into-mate, the exposure here is structural/positional (few immediate enemy checks) — the push creates long-term king weakness rather than allowing an instant mating attack.

0.label: POLYSEMANTIC. Peak (top 25%, act 10-34): best move CAPTURES THE ENEMY QUEEN, missed in a mutual-capture standoff — often wrong move-order or wrong recapturing piece (54% best-captures-queen, +17% rook). But upper/mid/low bands (75% of 462 firings) are overwhelmingly NON-captures (76-100%) — the queen is involved but it's not a clean missed-queen-capture. Named for the peak; flagged polysemantic because the lower-activation mass is a different, broader pattern (missed tactics / quiet errors involving the queen).

17.label: Best move captures a FREE (undefended) MINOR piece the player declined — bishop or knight, never rook/queen (14/20 minors: bishop 10, knight 4; 5 pawns; 0 majors). High-activation cohort: bishop 78%, knight 22%. A hanging minor left on the board, distinct from 'Missed Exchange' (trades) and major-piece blunders.

10.label: The move is almost always a capture/exchange (90% capture, 95% loses own material, 80% ends in a trade) that liquidates its last active or defending piece—often a rook—surrendering counterplay into a hopelessly lost endgame (best move instead keeps the piece active and wins material); TOP boards are decisive trades into resignable endgames or removed-defender mates (back-rank Rxe8#, Bxf7#), while MEDIAN boards are milder ~160–300cp positional/tactical slips (allowing a fork, trapping a knight, losing castling) that merely worsen an already difficult position rather than instantly losing.

13.label: In winning endgames the player repeatedly fails to grab a free hanging piece—usually the king (or a pawn) capturing a bishop/knight that blockades a passed pawn—and instead pushes a pawn or shuffles the king; top boards are clean missed king-captures that throw away a clearly won game (~650cp+ swings), while median boards degrade into subtler near-equal endgame slips (wrong pawn push, tempo loss, advancing the wrong passer) where no piece is truly hanging.

12.label: Self-inflicted material loss (hung-own 97%, refutation 4/4 confirm loss of 2-11 pts). The move that does it varies widely (pawn 39%, knight 27%, bishop 20%, rook 7%) and the amount lost ranges from a pawn to a full piece/exchange, so 'Hung Material' (broad) fits better than 'Hung Piece'. Opus: unblocks a diagonal, abandons a tactical resource, drops the exchange.

14.label: A missed free capture that occurs predominantly in the endgame (83% endgame by see_stats, 15/20 boards by piece count). Mostly FREE/undefended captures (13/20), rook-dominant (74% of cohort). Distinct from f17 (minor-piece, all phases) by being an endgame major-piece grab left on the board.

18.label: In 100% endgames the (78%) king is shuffled to the wrong square, abandoning a critical duty (pawn-support, blockade, or mating-net) and losing tempo/advantage; TOP boards squander outright forced mates/wins (Kf4, Kf8, Kf6 etc.), while MEDIAN boards are only minor king/rook missteps—often 0–60cp inaccuracies in already-decided positions.

15.label: The played move is a capture that backfires — you grab a piece/pawn and it loses material or initiative (played-capture ~96-100% at peak, hung-own 100%, outcome 'trade' 92%). The best move is usually a quiet developing move or castling, not a recapture. Holds across the full range (played-capture 30/30 top down to ~20/30 in the weak tail). Not a clean even trade — the capture itself is the mistake.

20.label: Best move attacks the enemy queen (tempo-gaining) on 20/20 peak+median boards; shortened from the verbose 'Missed Tempo-Gaining Queen Attack'.

22.label: In drawn/equal endgames the player makes a passive king or knight move instead of the one available material-winning capture; top boards are blatant free grabs of a hanging queen or rook (NxQ, KxR, Bxb2), while median boards soften into subtler king-placement endgame errors (wrong side, lost opposition, walking into a fork).

21.label: Player makes an unrelated developing/pawn move and leaves a knight en prise in the opening (lost own material 100%, opening 100%); top boards are textbook clean hangs of the f6/f3 knight to a pawn capture (exf6, gxf3, dxc3), while median boards loosen into knights lost via forks, trapped pieces, and other tactical oversights.

24.label: The best move is a quiet, non-capturing repositioning the player overlooked. Peak (act ~33): 10/10 forward central pawn breaks (d5/d4/e4/f4) that the player skipped for a passive move. Median (act ~13): broadens to backward piece repositioning — knight retreats/regroups (Nf4, Nb6, Ne4) and king steps, all backward moves. Unifying idea: improve your position with a quiet pawn-forward or piece-back move, not an active lunge.

8.label: There is a move (82% a capture, winning material ~79%) that grabs free/hanging material—frequently a loose rook—but the player instead makes a passive, trade-offering move (70% rook moves) that surrenders the win; in the TOP boards this is a blatant undefended piece (often a rook) left uncaptured for decisive or mating swings, whereas in the MEDIAN boards the overlooked capture is subtler and the passive move just allows a favorable simplifying trade or walks into a fork/mate-threat for smaller (~200–450cp) losses.

19.label: In its strongest activations the engine has a passed pawn ready to queen (best move is consistently a8=Q/c8=Q/h8=Q) but instead pushes a different pawn or shuffles the rook/king and squanders forced wins or mates; in median activations the signal degrades into more general endgame slips—misplacing the king or removing a key defender—where promotion is no longer the theme, so the team reads as 'Missed Promotion' fading into faulty endgame technique.

23.label: The player repeatedly chose a quiet, non-forcing move when the best move was a check (100% of boards) that should have been played immediately; top boards throw away short, immediate forced mates (mate in 1-7), while median boards miss a forcing check that wins material or only a longer/slower mate.

26.label: The player is winning and the best move is a capture/trade (19/20 best moves are captures, mostly queen/rook trades) that liquidates into a trivially won pawn/minor endgame — but they decline it, playing a pointless check, a passive shuffle, or a pawn push instead. Classic conversion failure: won't simplify into the won endgame. Confirmed by 3 independent Opus-4.8 analysts (high confidence, ~17/20 fit) + Sam. Sub-pattern: reflexive checks instead of the capturing trade.

25.label: Dual: the best move is an EQUAL TRADE the player declined (20/20 even exchanges, zero free captures) AND the move played instead HANGS material in the refutation (verified 3/3 on cached boards: end-of-line loss 9-12pts, Opus confirms 'Qxc5/Qxd1+/Qxe7 devastating'). You skipped a correct trade and dropped a piece. (refutation coverage thin: 3/20 cached + Opus text.)

16.chip: Exposed King, Queen Lost to Pin
16.label: The recurring mistake is neglecting king safety—making a greedy capture or non-prophylactic move that leaves the king exposed—where the top boards almost uniformly leave the king on the a7-g1 diagonal and lose the queen to a bishop pin/check (Bc5/Bd4), while the median boards generalize to a broadly exposed or uncastled king punished by diagonal checks (Qa5+/Qh4+), forks, and file pins that win various material.

32.label: The recurring error is voluntarily pushing/breaking a pawn (100% pawn moves, 86% endgames) that dissolves a locked or restraining structure, handing the opponent an outside passed pawn or counterplay when a quiet king move was correct; top positions are textbook pawn-endgame breaks (c4, b5, a5, d6) that release a decisive passer via recapture, whereas median positions degrade into more varied tempo-losing or weakening moves, including piece moves (Ra8, Bb4, Nf8) that merely surrender the defensive grip rather than instantly losing.

27.label: The player ignores an impending attack on its own king—removing a key defender (g7 pawn, defending knight/bishop) or making a passive/greedy move instead of the available defensive queen trade (best piece is the queen 89% of the time)—leaving the king exposed; top positions are forced checkmates (Rxd1#, Qg7#, Bg5+ fork) while median positions soften to winning attacks or material loss rather than immediate mate.

28.label: The player abandons a winning initiative by choosing a passive, materialistic, or trading move instead of the decisive attacking blow (most often a queen centralization like Qe5/Qe4/Qxh3 or a crushing sacrifice like Rxh7/Bf6), with the best move winning material 72% and being the queen 58% while delivering 0% checks; top boards squander outright forced mates and rook sacrifices (10k+ cp swings), whereas median boards merely miss the strong attacking move that would have preserved a big advantage or the initiative.

35.label: Player makes a routine recapture or natural move instead of inserting a tempo-gaining in-between capture; top boards are clean missed zwischenzugs that win a full piece (e.g., the routine 'Qxe2' instead of the intermediate Bxe7/Bxf6 exploiting mutual threats), while median boards broaden into general move-order errors and missed intermediate captures that merely squander the existing advantage.

34.label: The correct move is a pawn move 85% of the time (17/20 best moves are pawns, frequently the central break e5xd4 / e4xd5 / c4xd5) — the player instead played a piece move or wrong pawn move. A central-pawn-tension / pawn-play feature: the position calls for a pawn move and you didn't make the right one.

30.label: Player voluntarily gives up a piece for a pawn in an unsound attack (best move was quiet, capture-best only 2%, lost own material 100%); top boards are textbook bad bishop sacs against the king (Bxh3/Bxh6/Bxg6 for one pawn that just gets recaptured), while median boards broaden into general self-inflicted material losses and hung/overlooked pieces.

33.label: The player makes a developing/quiet move that lets an enemy pawn advance win material—either trapping a bishop or forking two pieces—almost always in the opening; top boards are clean flank-pawn (a/b/c-pawn) bishop traps that simply win the bishop, while median boards shift toward central pawn-break forks (e5/d4) that hit the f6-knight plus a second piece (or, more rarely, other tactical motifs the same prophylaxis would have prevented).

31.label: The best move is an EQUAL TRADE the player declined (20/20 even exchanges — bishopxknight, queenxqueen, rookxrook, pawnxpawn; zero free/hanging captures). Distinct from 'Missed Capture' (a free undefended piece) — every capture here is defended/recaptured.

39.label: The player consistently moves the king (90%) to a losing square; in the TOP positions these are endgame king-marches that head the wrong way—failing to capture a passed pawn, support its own pawns, or gain a checking tempo—whereas in the MEDIAN positions the error shifts to king-safety blunders where the move exposes the king to decisive checks or mate.

36.label: In winning/equal endgames the player fails to neutralize the opponent's passed pawn—pushing the wrong pawn, capturing the wrong pawn, or moving the king/piece off the blockade and so losing the promotion race; top boards are catastrophic won→lost blunders (missed mate or letting the pawn queen with a tempo-gaining check), while median boards are smaller king-and-pawn missteps that merely squander the win or let a draw slip.

42.label: Clean self-inflicted hang: the played move leaves the player's own material en prise (hung-own 100%; refutation confirms material loss 3/3). Opus: 'moved the queen to an undefended square', 'pawn push ignoring the undefended queen'. Queen-dominant at peak (53%) but broadens to rook/pawn/knight, so 'Hung Piece' not 'Hung Queen'.

47.label: In every position the best move was a forcing check that the player overlooked (often grabbing material or making a quiet move instead); top boards are all missed forced checkmates (mate-in-1 to mate-in-8), while median boards are missed shorter mates or winning/tempo-gaining checks that merely squander a large advantage rather than an outright mate.

40.label: The player moves the piece that was the SOLE/critical defender — of the king's mating squares, the back rank, or a passed-pawn blockade — either to grab material (greed) or to retreat passively (fear). The undefended square then collapses, usually to mate. Queen is the repeat offender but it recurs with rooks (back-rank/blockade), bishops (king diagonal), even a pawn (gxf5 removing the only stop to Qg7#). Consensus of 4 independent Opus-4.8 analysts (high confidence, ~15/20 fit; clean greed-vs-retreat sub-split). NOT a queen trade. Outliers: wrong-piece captures, king-into-fork (~5 tail).

43.label: The player (usually with a king move) overlooks a free capture of an undefended major piece, throwing away a winning position; the top boards are clean missed grabs of a hanging rook or queen (best move a winning capture 100%), while the median boards degrade into king moves that instead walk into forks or mating nets rather than a simple capture.

37.label: In a winning/equal position the player overlooks the forcing best-move capture (best move is a capture 100%, often a pointless check or quiet king move played instead), throwing away the game; the top boards miss snatching the enemy QUEEN for free (huge 800–1000+cp/mate swings), while the median boards 'merely' miss capturing a rook, knight, or piece.

48.label: An unsound piece-for-pawn sacrifice on the f-square in the opening that is simply refuted by the king capturing (Kxf7/Kxf2) with no follow-up attack; top boards are bishop sacrifices on f7 (Bxf7+), while median boards shift toward knight sacrifices on f2/f7 (Nxf2).

41.label: The recurring mistake is playing a quiet/passive move (0% checks played) instead of the single forcing resource—an intermediate check, tactical capture, or zwischenzug that wins material or saves the game (best move wins material 100%, was a check 40% / capture 60%); TOP boards are sharp decisive misses (Rxf7!, Qg8+ perpetual, Qc1+/Rb2+ zwischenzugs, hanging-piece captures), while MEDIAN boards soften into passive positional and king-safety lapses (wrong-way king moves, surrendering castling, slow developing moves).

29.label: A middlegame feature (94% middlegame) where the player both hangs their own material (lost-own ~88%) and overlooks a winning capture — the decisive move is a forcing check/capture (best-is-check 88%, wins material 100%) on essentially every board. Direction is genuinely mixed: some boards you hung a piece, others you missed taking one.

38.label: Sharp positions where A king is under attack — yours or the opponent's — and the player plays a check into it (played-check 100%). At peak the ENEMY king is the hot one (pressure avg 2.1, you're attacking); lower bands shift toward your OWN king exposed. A king is under fire (>=2 attackers) on ~70-80% of boards every band. Not a specific tactic — a king-danger position detector.

50.label: The recurring mistake is voluntarily placing/moving a bishop onto an undefended square—usually a greedy pawn-grab capture (Bxc7, Bxb7, Bxg7, Bxa6, Bxh3)—where it is immediately recaptured for free, losing a full piece for a pawn; the top activations are pure 'hung bishop' opening blunders (bishop 100%, lost own material 100%, eval crashing to ~-450), while the median activations decay into a grab-bag of unrelated middlegame/endgame errors (king-safety walks, back-rank/fork oversights, positional slips) where the specific hung-bishop theme largely disappears.

44.label: Player either steps the king onto an open file/diagonal or fails to make the prophylactic king-safety move (best move is a king move 67% of the time, e.g. Kh1/Ka8/Kh8), unleashing a discovered check or back-rank shot; TOP boards lose the queen outright to the discovery (mostly Nc6+/Rf-file discoveries), while MEDIAN boards instead walk the exposed king into a forced mate or crushing king-side attack.

54.label: A missed tactical motif that wins material — fork OR pin, by whichever piece. Peak boards are mostly knight forks (Nf2/Ne2/Nd6) but already include a bishop fork (g4f5); median broadens to rook pins-to-king (f1e1 pinning a knight, allowing a free capture), bishop forks (g7b2, f8b4), and rook lifts. Piece distribution knight 11 / bishop 4 / rook 3 / pawn 2 — so the invariant is the missed fork-or-pin tactic, NOT 'knight'.

55.label: The player overlooks a winning knight tactic—usually a fork delivered with check that nets a piece or the exchange (best move is a check 82%, wins material 95%, best piece knight 57%); top boards are razor-sharp missed knight forks (Nf4+, Ne2+, Ne6+, Nf5+, Ne4+) winning clean material, whereas median boards degrade into vaguer missed best-moves—tempo losses, passive king-safety slips and positional errors—where no crisp fork is present.

52.label: Player neglects the opponent's most urgent threat—overwhelmingly an enemy passed pawn racing to promote—and instead grabs a tempting but irrelevant capture/check ('patzer sees a check'); top boards are clear-cut, pawn-on-7th immediate-queening blunders, while median boards are softer cases of allowing a passed pawn to be created/advance or other neglected threats (hung pieces, king safety).

45.label: The player moves/leaves the queen so the opponent can force an unfavorable queen exchange (88% queen moves) that dissolves the player's only resource — in the TOP boards the trade dumps White/Black straight into a hopelessly lost (usually pawn) endgame by surrendering perpetual-check or attacking chances, while in the MEDIAN boards the same wrong-time queen trade or retreat merely throws away a winning attack or an outright forced mate.

59.label: The played move lets the opponent give check — 99/100 boards across all activation bands allow a checking reply. At strong activations these checks are a forced mate (top band 24/25 forced-mate ≤5ply, classic Qxh7#/diagonal mates); in the weaker tail they soften to damaging checks / king-safety collapses short of forced mate. Mirror of 'Missed Check/Mate' (f47): there you skipped your own check, here your move hands the opponent one.

57.label: Sharp positions where a king is exposed (a king under fire, >=2 attackers, on 9/10 peak / 7/10 median — usually the ENEMY king, pressure ~2.9). No check played (0%), queen-led maneuvers (67%) but broadens to bishop/knight/rook — so 'King Exposed' not 'Unsound Queen Attack'. Distinct from f38 'King in Danger' which is checking INTO the danger (played-check 100%); f57 is king-exposed without a check.

51.label: The player keeps overlooking a critical capture of a hanging enemy piece (usually a rook or queen, best move is a capture 81% / wins material 88%) and instead drifts with a passive king or pawn move that loses; in the TOP boards the missed grab would have taken the enemy queen/rook and dodged forced mate (total collapse), while in the MEDIAN boards the missed capture is smaller or comes in already-lost king-safety positions where it merely deepens the loss.

53.label: A self-inflicted material loss driven by a knight move (78% knight, 89% lost own material)—either parking the knight on a square where it's captured for free or trading it off badly; TOP boards are catastrophic, the knight move hanging major material (queen/rook) or walking into forced mate with ~300-700cp swings, while MEDIAN boards just drop the knight itself or make a small bad knight trade (and several are near-non-blunders).

61.label: The player overlooks a forced checkmate—almost always a queen check (best move is a check 100% of the time)—and instead grabs a routine capture or makes a king/retreat move; top boards are stark mate-in-one shots (Qxb7#, Qxg7#, Rxd1#) blown by reflex captures, while median boards are longer or move-order-sensitive forced mates squandered by the wrong check, a passive tempo-losing move, or a missed in-between, leaving the side still winning but no longer mating.

62.label: A forcing queen check (Qa4+/Qa5+/Qh4+/Qh5+) that wins a full piece is overlooked in favor of a slow developing move; top boards are textbook missed winning checks against an uncastled king in the opening, while median boards decay into vaguer non-forcing positional/tempo errors where the best move is no longer a winning queen check.

46.label: The player grabs material (a fork, a pinned piece, or a pawn) instead of first dealing with a threat to their own queen, allowing a stronger counter-capture; in the TOP boards this literally hangs the queen to a bishop intermezzo (…Bxd1/Bxd8 after the player captures elsewhere), while in the MEDIAN boards the same greed costs only a lesser piece or a tempo (queen chased by Nc3, bishop lost to Rxe2, etc.) rather than the full queen.

60.label: In losing, king-exposed positions the player overlooks the one saving/tempo-gaining check (often a perpetual or delaying check) and instead plays a passive or king-walking move that allows forced mate (best move is a check 100% of the time); the TOP boards are longer forced mates where the missed check would have prolonged resistance or held a perpetual, whereas the MEDIAN boards are sharper, immediate back-rank or mate-in-2 collapses where the missed check/interposition was the only survival.

63.label: In near-pure pawn endgames the player burns the one critical tempo with a slow, passive move (usually a king retreat or wrong flank push) instead of the decisive passed-pawn advance/breakthrough or promotion race — top boards are clear-cut king dawdling that throws away a forced winning pawn break (e5/e7/g6/d7/c6), while median boards are messier and smaller-swing, mixing rook/knight tempo-losses and failures to push or blockade a passer.

58.label: In winning endgames the player gives a queen/rook capture-or-check that simply gets recaptured (best move never a capture), sacrificing a major piece for a pawn and frequently dropping the win — top boards are the most severe, converting clear wins into dead draws via insufficient mating material (K+B vs K, K vs K), while median boards are lower-stakes, more mixed blunders that instead allow the opponent's forks/mating nets rather than directly hanging your own queen.

56.label: The player initiates a capture/trade (70% a bishop) that backfires, letting the opponent recapture into a dominant central queen or a winning fork/check and surrendering a won position; top boards are clean bishop trades that hand the enemy queen a crushing central post (d4/d5/c6/e3), while median boards degrade into cruder material drops where a piece or pawn is simply left hanging.

49.label: The played move attacks the enemy queen (chasing it for tempo) but it's a mistake — the attacking piece hangs or the tempo is wasted. Constant across nearly all boards (top 25/25, upper 24/25, mid 22/25 played-move-attacks-queen); the attacking piece varies (pawn/knight/bishop/rook), so it's the queen-harassment that's the invariant, not the piece. Low-activation tail loosens into other loose-piece moves.
